title: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks
one_liner: Measure whether an agent can carry lessons from one session into later sessions where success depends on what it learned earlier.
lead: Many memory tests ask whether an agent can repeat a fact from earlier text. Real work is harder. An agent may need to learn a preference in one session, notice a mistake in a second session, and use both facts days later to finish a larger task. MemoryArena targets that long chain. It builds multi-session tasks where earlier actions create information that later actions depend on, so the evaluation measures useful memory rather than short-term recall alone.

problem.h2: Why recall-only memory tests miss the hard part
paras: A recall test asks whether the agent can retrieve an earlier fact. A single-session action test asks whether the agent can finish a task now. Neither one captures the setting where an agent must learn while acting and then use that learned material in later sessions. In practice, those pieces are coupled because many future choices only make sense if the agent remembers what happened before.

That gap creates misleading optimism. A system can do well on long-context recall and still fail a real multi-session job because it does not store the right experiences, does not compress them into a useful memory, or does not consult that memory when later choices depend on it.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build multi-session tasks with explicit dependence between subtasks so that an agent must learn from earlier interactions and use that memory later to finish the full job.

steps.text: Create tasks where one session reveals information that another session must use so that memory is necessary, not optional.
Let the agent act, observe outcomes, and receive feedback across multiple sessions instead of one uninterrupted prompt.
Agents can record summaries or notes so that the benchmark tests how well they build useful long-term records.
Check whether downstream actions use earlier experience correctly because memory quality only matters if it changes future behavior.
Evaluate on web tasks, planning, search, and formal reasoning so that the benchmark reveals whether memory strategies transfer across settings.

paras: The paper changes memory evaluation from static recall into action-guiding memory across time. It asks whether past experience becomes useful state for future decisions.
object.object: What counts as good memory for an agent

hidden.name: How much decision-useful information from earlier sessions survives into later ones
paras: The key hidden quantity is not how many words from the past the agent can repeat. It is how much task-relevant state survives into the next session in a form the agent can actually use. A weak memory system may store too much, too little, or the wrong detail, so later actions drift even when the earlier experience contained the answer.

MemoryArena surfaces this quantity by creating explicit causal links between sessions. Because later subtasks depend on earlier discoveries, the benchmark can identify whether failure came from poor observation, poor storage, poor retrieval, or poor later use.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark places where task-relevant memory can break before the final answer.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much of the earlier lesson stays available in a useful form for later action.
MemoryArena evaluates memory inside multi-session agent loops where later subtasks depend explicitly on state learned earlier.

paras: The benchmark works because it ties memory to future consequences. If later subtasks are independent, then an agent can ignore history and still score well. By making earlier sessions informative for later ones, MemoryArena ensures that memory quality directly affects task completion.

The domain diversity also matters because a memory method that helps on one setting may fail on another. A note-taking strategy that works for web navigation may be poor for sequential reasoning if it stores surface details instead of decision rules.

Grader checks whether memory changed the later action

math.words: Score an agent by how well it stores useful information from earlier sessions and how well it uses that information when later subtasks depend on it.
math.equation: score = w_store * store_quality + w_use * use_quality ; final_success <= use_quality
symbols: overall score for one multi-session task
how well the saved memory captures the facts that later subtasks need
how well the later action applies the saved memory when choosing what to do
weight on building a useful memory record
weight on applying that record later
1 if the whole interdependent task is completed correctly, else 0

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: In session one, a user says they dislike red-eye flights and prefer aisle seats.
A good memory record keeps both facts because both can affect a later booking choice.
Suppose store_quality = 0.9 because both preferences were saved clearly.
In session two, the agent books a daytime aisle flight, so use_quality = 1.0.
If the agent had saved only the aisle-seat fact and ignored the time preference, use_quality would fall because the final booking could violate the earlier lesson.
The benchmark rewards the second step most heavily because memory matters only when it guides later action.

math.note: The paper measures full benchmark performance across task families, but this simplified equation captures its core principle: good memory must be both stored and used.

charts.title: Recall-heavy tests
charts.note: Strong scores on simpler tests do not transfer automatically because useful memory in action requires more than retrieval.

charts.title: MemoryArena message
rows: Confidence that old tests are enough
charts.note: The paper's main result is a mismatch between easy recall benchmarks and harder interdependent tasks because later decisions expose whether memory is truly useful.

items.html: If the memory record grows without selection, later retrieval can become noisy because important facts are buried among irrelevant ones.

items.b: A task may reward recall more than action.
items.html: If a later subtask depends only weakly on earlier sessions, the benchmark may understate the real memory challenge because the connection is too loose.

items.b: Later failures can have many causes.
items.html: A bad downstream action may come from weak planning rather than weak memory, so diagnostic analysis matters because not every miss is a storage problem.
Use subtasks with explicit dependence and inspect both stored notes and later choices so that memory failures can be localized cleanly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a three-session travel assistant task. In session one, the user states preferences. In session two, the agent learns from a failed booking attempt. In session three, the agent must complete a new booking that depends on both the old preferences and the lesson from the failure. Compare an agent with no explicit memory, one with naive note storage, and one with curated memory summaries.
The demo should show that later task success rises only when the agent stores the right lessons and retrieves them at decision time, because memory that never affects action is not useful memory.
demo.closing: The benchmark is asking a practical question: can the agent turn past experience into better future choices by storing the parts that later decisions depend on?
